result.summary: The Chorus sings of women who destroyed their kin or husbands, then says Justice and Vengeance are bringing Orestes home. Orestes, disguised as a Phocian stranger, comes to the palace and tells Clytaemestra that Orestes is dead.

scenes.title: Chorus on women's crimes
scenes.summary: The Chorus recalls Althaea, Scylla and the Lemnian women as examples of terrible deeds. It ends by saying Justice and Vengeance are bringing the son home.

scenes.title: Orestes' false news
scenes.summary: Orestes, in disguise, knocks and is received by Clytaemestra. He says a man named Strophius asked him to report Orestes' death, and she welcomes him as a guest.
scenes.stakes: Orestes risks discovery while gaining entry to the house of his enemies.

notable_quotes.reason: Vivid image of Justice, announcing coming vengeance.

analysis.text: The ode links female crime to the house's curse while promising that Justice will repay old bloodshed.
Orestes' disguise and false news of his death deceive Clytaemestra, as Apollo's plan requires.

language_notes.text: "Lights hung aloft" refers to meteors and fiery phenomena in the sky, listed among the world's terrors.
"Twixt" is a contraction of "betwixt," meaning between.
Althaea, daughter of Thestius, burned the brand on which her son Meleager's life depended, after he killed her brothers.
This is Scylla, daughter of Nisus king of Megara, who cut her father's magic lock of hair, bribed by Minos, on whom the city's safety depended.
"Reft" is the archaic past tense of "reave," to seize or rob.
Hermes, as guide of the dead, overtook Nisus: he died after his daughter's betrayal.
The Lemnian women killed their husbands on the island of Lemnos; "Lemnian deeds" became a byword for atrocity.
"If by Aegisthus' will it offers welcome" means: if the house, under Aegisthus' rule, receives strangers at all. Orestes pointedly names the usurper.
"Drop anchor" is a sailing image for stopping at an inn; "the car of Night" pictures Night as a chariot.
Daulis was a town in Phocis, central Greece. Phocis is where Orestes was secretly raised, so his false identity stays close to the truth.
The bronze urn of ashes is the invented proof of death; Greeks cremated the dead and kept the ashes in urns.
The Curse is the inherited doom on the house of Atreus, here treated as a hunter that strikes from afar.

context_notes.text: Orestes, Pylades and Electra leave to carry out the plan to kill Clytemnestra; the Chorus of libation-bearing women fills the interval with song.
The "marriage void of love" is Clytemnestra's with Agamemnon, whom she killed on his return from Troy.
The "son" is Orestes, who returns to avenge his father Agamemnon's murder.
Orestes has returned to Argos in secret to avenge his father Agamemnon. Pylades is his loyal friend, who barely speaks in the play.
Orestes asks for the master, Aegisthus, since he intends to kill him. Clytaemestra, Orestes' mother, answers instead.
Strophius was king of Phocis and Pylades' father. In the tradition he sheltered the young Orestes in exile.

literary_notes.text: The song opens with a list of natural terrors, building toward the claim that human, especially female, passion is worse.
"Dog-hearted" condemns Scylla as shameless and ruthless in a single compound image.
The Chorus asks whether its examples are fair, pressing the audience to apply them to Clytemnestra.
Justice as an anvil and Destiny as a smith forging a sword present vengeance as fixed and inevitable.
Vengeance is imagined as a brooding spirit leading Orestes home, foreshadowing the coming matricide.
The audience knows the speaker is Orestes, so he delivers news of his own death to his mother, who does not recognize him.
The Curse is imagined as an archer whose arrows reach far, so even those sent to safety are struck.
Orestes' courteous question flatters his hosts and hides his purpose, helping him keep up the disguise.
Clytaemestra's plan to tell the master leads to Aegisthus coming unguarded, which sets up his death.
